speaker: David Chang
title: Chef David Chang (Momofuku): “I’m Addicted to Creative Excitement”
question: In restaurant kitchens, why do talented cooks so often struggle when they move into managing people?
guest: In cooking, it's funny, and I can't speak on behalf of other businesses, but if you're really talented at it or if you're good at it, you get promoted. And it's weird because you don't learn... Nobody teaches communication. Nobody teaches how to resolve a crisis in a thoughtful way. It just was an unprofessionalized environment, and a lot of it was just carried on from previous generations. And that was sort of the kitchen culture, and a lot of it was celebrated.

points.core: Kitchens promote cooks based solely on technical cooking skill.
points.note: Accept: advancing cooks into leadership because they excel at cooking/station execution rather than people-management aptitude. Do not credit: vague claims that 'chefs have big egos.'

points.core: Chefs receive no formal training in people management skills.
points.note: Accept: lack of instruction in communication, thoughtful crisis resolution, or leadership inside an unprofessionalized workplace. Do not credit: merely saying 'kitchens are stressful' without noting the absence of management training.

points.core: Harsh management habits are inherited from previous kitchen generations.
points.note: Accept: generational transmission of abrasive kitchen norms passed down from earlier chefs and brigades. Do not credit: attributing bad management purely to individual personality flaws.

points.core: Traditional kitchen culture actively celebrates aggressive management styles.
points.note: Accept: hospitality culture glorifying, rewarding, or romanticizing yelling and harshness as signs of rigor. Do not credit: claiming harshness is only an accidental byproduct of busy shifts.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Mostly because the skills that earn the promotion are almost the opposite of the skills the new job requires. A great line cook succeeds through personal speed, precision, and control: when something is going wrong, they fix it with their own hands. Managing means getting results through other people, which requires delegating, teaching, tolerating someone else's slower or imperfect work, and giving feedback, none of which the line ever trained them to do.

Several things compound this. Kitchens usually promote the best cook, not the best teacher, and offer little or no management training. The new chef often learned under a harsh, hierarchical brigade culture, so they default to yelling or to jumping in and doing the job themselves, which leaves the team undeveloped and the chef burned out. They are also suddenly supervising former peers, which makes holding people accountable awkward.

Finally, the job itself changes: scheduling, food and labor costs, ordering, hiring, and conflict resolution replace cooking. Many find they have lost the part of the work they loved and were good at, in exchange for work no one prepared them for.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Restaurant kitchens routinely promote their fastest, most consistent line cooks into sous-chef or head-chef roles, assuming culinary excellence translates into leadership. In practice, the two jobs require nearly opposite skills. Great cooking rewards individual speed, sensory precision, and direct physical control, whereas managing a kitchen demands delegation, patience, emotional regulation, and administrative discipline like scheduling and food costing.

Because restaurants rarely provide formal management training, newly promoted chefs must improvise under intense service pressure. Cooks who built their identity on personal execution often struggle to let go, stepping in to redo tasks themselves rather than coaching slower staff, which fuels burnout and resentment. Transitioning from peer to boss also strains tight-knit line relationships. Finally, many talented cooks came up under volatile, authoritarian chefs; without healthier leadership models, they tend either to mimic that harshness or overcorrect into conflict avoidance, leaving kitchen standards inconsistent and their team unsupported.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Talented cooks usually get promoted for being great at the work itself, and managing a kitchen is a different job. A line cook succeeds through personal speed, precision and stamina. A sous or head chef succeeds by getting results through other people. That means delegating, teaching, scheduling, costing and handling conflict, and almost nobody trains cooks in any of it.

Kitchen culture makes the gap worse. Many chefs learned under the old brigade style, where yelling, shaming and "figure it out" were normal, so they copy what was done to them. Under pressure, the instinct is to jump on the station and fix things yourself. That feels productive, but it undermines the cooks and leaves no one steering the whole service. High personal standards can also become impatience with slower learners.

Identity is part of it too. A cook's pride comes from what they put on the plate, and management pays off in less visible ways: lower turnover, steady food costs, a team that runs well without you. On top of that, long hours, thin margins and constant staffing churn leave little time to learn new skills, so many new managers fall back on what they already do best: cooking.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Talented cooks often struggle as managers because the skills that earn a promotion in a kitchen are almost the opposite of the skills needed to run one. Line cooking rewards individual speed, precision, and hands-on control; management requires stepping back, delegating, and getting results through other people. Because restaurants rarely offer formal leadership training, newly promoted sous chefs and head chefs are usually thrown into scheduling, labor budgets, inventory, and conflict resolution with little preparation. The shift from peer to boss also complicates kitchen dynamics, making it difficult to hold former teammates accountable without damaging morale or overcompensating with harsh authority. Under the intense, immediate pressure of a busy service, the instinct is to jump back on the line and fix mistakes personally rather than coach someone through them. That habit solves the moment's crisis, but it prevents the team from growing, creates bottlenecks, and quickly leads to exhaustion and resentment.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Talented cooks are often promoted because they can run a station under pressure. Managing a kitchen asks them to get that same consistency from a whole crew. That means making expectations explicit, teaching people with different levels of experience, giving feedback, and handling conflict. A cook can spend years getting better at the craft with little chance to practice those skills.

The pace of service can make the transition harder. When tickets pile up, taking over a struggling cook’s station may be the right call. If that becomes the default, though, the cook misses a chance to learn and the manager becomes the person everyone depends on to fix things. The shift is from knowing how to get a dish right yourself to helping other people get it right reliably, even when you’re across the kitchen.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A talented cook can rescue a busy service by stepping onto a station and doing the work. A kitchen manager has to help the person on that station handle the next rush, too. That takes a different set of skills. A cook who spots a sauce about to split may struggle to explain what tipped them off. A manager has to put that judgment into words, give feedback someone can use, and leave them room to try again.

During a rush, taking over can be the right call. When it becomes a habit, the crew gets less practice and the manager ends up doing every difficult job. Kitchens often promote cooks for speed, consistency, and composure before they’ve had much chance to practice teaching, delegating, or handling conflict. The promotion recognizes skills they’ve already proved while asking them to learn a new job in the middle of service.
